lead: A large language model is a decoder-only transformer trained on a very large text corpus to predict the next token. Scaling parameters, data and compute gives a general generator that can answer, summarise, translate and write code from a prompt. It produces text one token at a time, and a decoding rule chooses each token from the model's probability distribution. Chat assistants, code helpers and voice assistants use this loop.
prereq: You need: 6.4 for the transformer decoder and self-attention, and 6.3 for the encoder-decoder view of generation.

blocks.text: A model's size is its number of parameters, the learned weights. Large language models have billions. Three quantities scale together: parameters, training tokens and compute. Scaling behaviour means training loss falls smoothly as each grows, so builders scale all three.

A token is a piece of text, not always a word. Byte-pair encoding (BPE) starts from characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair. Common words become one token; rare words split into subword pieces. This keeps the vocabulary finite and handles new words.

Pretraining uses a decoder-only transformer from 6.4. The task is next-token prediction: given x₁ to xₜ₋₁, predict xₜ. A causal mask stops a position seeing later tokens. No human labels are needed because the next token is the label.

blocks.where: L is the training loss; xₜ is the token at position t; P is the model's probability for the true next token.

blocks.text: History runs from word vectors (Unit 5) to RNNs (6.2) to transformers, then to scaled chat models such as GPT-3, GPT-4 and Llama. Some are closed, some have open weights.

sections.h3: Prompts, in-context learning and instruction tuning

blocks.text: A prompt is the text handed to the model: an instruction, context, examples or all three. Prompting works because pretraining teaches continuation patterns. In-context learning means the model picks up a task from examples inside the prompt without changing weights. Zero-shot gives no example; one-shot gives one; few-shot gives a few. Two labelled sentiment reviews, for example, can set the format for a third.

Instruction tuning fine-tunes the pretrained model on instruction-response pairs. It changes behaviour: the model learns to follow requests. It does not change the tokenizer or add new facts to the weights. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) goes further: people rank outputs, a reward model learns the ranking, and reinforcement learning adjusts the model.
A chatbot wraps this generator in a dialogue loop and keeps recent turns as context. A voice assistant adds speech recognition and synthesis; see Unit 7.
At each step the transformer outputs a logit zᵢ for every token i in the vocabulary. Softmax turns logits into probabilities. Temperature T divides the logits first.
pᵢ = exp(zᵢ / T) ÷ Σⱼ exp(zⱼ / T)
blocks.where: pᵢ is the probability of token i; zᵢ is its logit; T is the temperature, a positive number; the sum runs over all vocabulary tokens.

blocks.text: T > 1 flattens the distribution: probability spreads toward unlikely tokens, so output is more random. T < 1 sharpens it: the largest logit dominates, so output is more repetitive. T = 1 leaves the softmax unchanged. T → 0 approaches greedy decoding, and T = 0 is not a valid division. Greedy picks the highest-probability token. Beam search keeps B best partial sequences and scores them by summed log probability. Sampling draws from p. top-k keeps the k highest tokens and renormalises. top-p keeps the smallest set whose cumulative probability reaches p and renormalises; it adapts to flat or sharp distributions.
Low temperature and top-p reduce wild output, but do not remove hallucination: fluent text that is false. Greedy decoding often repeats phrases.

Perplexity is PP = exp(−(1/N) Σ ln p(wₜ)), where N is the number of tokens and p(wₜ) is the probability the model gave the true token. Lower is better, and values compare only under the same tokenizer. Task accuracy uses exact match or F1. Translation uses BLEU (6.6). Human preference compares two outputs side by side.

spec.title: Next token: T = 0.5, then top-2
spec.aria: A table of one decoding step for tokens A, B, C, D: logits 2.0, 1.0, 0.5, −1.0 divided by 0.5 give 4.0, 2.0, 1.0, −2.0; softmax gives probabilities 0.842, 0.114, 0.042, 0.002; top-2 keeps A and B and renormalises them to 0.881 and 0.119.

examples.question: A next-token step gives logits [2.0, 1.0, 0.5, −1.0] for four tokens A, B, C, D. Decode with temperature T = 0.5, then keep the top 2 tokens. Find the four probabilities after temperature and the two probabilities after top-2 renormalisation.
examples.answer: After T = 0.5 the probabilities are [0.842, 0.114, 0.042, 0.002]; after top-2 they are [0.881, 0.119].
examples.check:
import math
z = [2.0, 1.0, 0.5, -1.0]
T = 0.5
e = [math.exp(v / T) for v in z]
Z = sum(e)
p = [v / Z for v in e]
for v in p:
    print(f"{v:.3f}")
top2 = p[:2]
s = sum(top2)
for v in top2:
    print(f"{v / s:.3f}")

traps: Temperature divides logits before softmax. T = 0 means greedy decoding, not a legal division.
top-k keeps exactly k tokens; top-p keeps the smallest set whose cumulative probability reaches p. They are not the same rule.
Instruction tuning changes behaviour, not the tokenizer and not the facts stored in the weights.
Perplexity is per-token and lower is better; it is not task accuracy and is comparable only under the same tokenizer.
Beam search returns a high-probability sequence, not a guaranteed correct or factual one.

quiz.q: What is a token, and why do large language models use BPE instead of whole words?
quiz.a: A token is a piece of text, often a subword. BPE keeps the vocabulary finite and represents rare or new words as several pieces.

quiz.q: What does temperature do to the next-token distribution?
quiz.a: It divides the logits by T before softmax. T > 1 makes the distribution flatter and output more random; T < 1 makes it sharper and output more repetitive; T = 1 changes nothing.

quiz.q: Four logits are [0, 0, 0, 0]. With T = 1 and top-2, give the probabilities before and after renormalisation.
quiz.a: Equal logits give equal softmax probabilities 0.25 each. Top-2 keeps two tokens; renormalising gives 0.25/0.5 = 0.5 for each.

quiz.q: Why can top-p adapt better than top-k when the next-token distribution is flat?
quiz.a: A flat distribution spreads probability over many tokens. top-p then keeps more tokens to reach the chosen mass; top-k always keeps the same count and may cut likely tokens or keep unlikely ones.

quiz.q: State the difference between zero-shot, one-shot and few-shot prompting.
quiz.a: Zero-shot gives no worked example; one-shot gives one example; few-shot gives a small number of examples inside the prompt.

quiz.q: A model has average negative log-likelihood 0.693 per token. Find its perplexity.
quiz.a: Perplexity = exp(0.693) ≈ 2.0. The model behaves like a uniform choice over about two tokens at each step.

quiz.q: Instruction tuning changes behaviour but not the knowledge in the weights. Explain.
quiz.a: The tuning data teaches the format of following requests and preferring helpful answers. The pretraining corpus still supplies the facts; no new tokenizer or large body of facts is added.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern systems add retrieval-augmented generation (6.8) so the model reads documents before answering. Tool use lets a model call a calculator or search API. Evaluation now includes adversarial prompts, bias and safety. Efficient inference uses quantisation, distillation and cached key-value states. Search terms: scaling laws, LoRA, RLHF, speculative decoding, RAG.
